imageAlt: B-52 Stratofortress dropping bombs over Vietnam during Operation Linebacker II, December 1972
imageCaption: A B-52 Stratofortress during operations over Southeast Asia. During Operation Linebacker II, December 18-29, 1972, B-52s flew 729 sorties against targets in Hanoi and Haiphong.

longForm.title: Operation Linebacker II: Strategic Bombing, the Paris Talks, and a Debate That Has Not Been Settled
longForm.excerpt: In December 1972, Nixon ordered B-52s to bomb Hanoi and Haiphong for eleven days. The Paris Peace Accords followed twenty-nine days later. Whether those two facts are causally connected is one of the central unresolved questions of the air war in Vietnam.
paragraphs: On the evening of December 18, 1972, eighty-seven B-52 Stratofortresses lifted off from Andersen Air Force Base on Guam and U-Tapao Royal Thai Navy Airfield in Thailand. They flew in three waves toward Hanoi and Haiphong — the first strategic bombing of North Vietnam's heartland since Operation Rolling Thunder had ended in 1968. The crews had been briefed on the target list and the threat environment. They had not been briefed on the strategic context: that the Paris Peace negotiations had collapsed earlier that month, that Nixon had given Hanoi a seventy-two-hour ultimatum to return to the table, and that when Hanoi did not respond, the President had ordered Strategic Air Command to commence what would become eleven days of the most concentrated bombing of the war. The men flying those aircraft understood the operational mission. The political architecture behind it was above their classification level. It would be some years before the relationship between what happened in December 1972 and the Paris Peace Accords signed January 27, 1973 was examined with enough distance to be argued about properly.

The negotiations that preceded Linebacker II require careful treatment. Henry Kissinger had announced on October 26, 1972 that peace was at hand — a characterization that embarrassed both the Nixon administration and the South Vietnamese government, which had not agreed to the terms Kissinger described. The talks resumed in November and broke down in December, with both sides blaming the other. Nixon's private communications, preserved in the FRUS record, indicate that he had decided to resume heavy bombing before the deadline he gave Hanoi had technically expired — that the decision was driven as much by the calculation that bombing would strengthen the American negotiating position as by any expectation that Hanoi would actually comply with the ultimatum. That distinction matters because one of the central historiographical disputes about Linebacker II concerns whether it produced the agreement signed in January 1973, or whether that agreement would have been reached anyway, and the bombing was the political price Nixon needed to extract from Congress and from the South Vietnamese government of Nguyen Van Thieu to make the deal possible.

The first night's losses established that the operation had a tactical problem. Three B-52s were shot down on December 18 by North Vietnamese SA-2 Guideline surface-to-air missiles, with two more lost on December 19. The SA-2 had been in the North Vietnamese arsenal since 1965, and American electronic countermeasures had adapted to it repeatedly over the intervening years. The problem in December 1972 was not the missile itself but the tactics that Strategic Air Command had developed for the B-52 — tactics designed for the nuclear strike mission in Europe, not for high-threat conventional bombing. The post-target turns that B-52s executed after bomb release were predictable in timing and geometry. North Vietnamese radar operators had been trained to anticipate them. The SA-2 operators fired on the turn, where the aircraft's electronic countermeasures were partially degraded and the radar cross-section was largest. SAC headquarters in Omaha, which had retained control over the mission planning in a manner that left the on-scene Air Force commanders with limited flexibility, had not adjusted for this specific vulnerability.

The losses prompted an internal debate within the Air Force that the subsequent record documents with some candor. Brigadier General Glenn Sullivan, the on-scene commander at U-Tapao, recommended changes to the routing and altitude profiles that would make the aircraft less predictable. SAC headquarters, concerned about maintaining formation integrity and the effectiveness of the jamming pods — which were calibrated for specific aircraft spacings — resisted changes that would alter the standard formation. After the loss of six B-52s in the first three days — a rate that SAC's own analysis showed was unsustainable — the routing was altered. Post-target turns were varied. Aircraft approached from different headings on successive nights. The loss rate dropped significantly after December 21. The adaptation was real, but the question that the Air Force's own post-operation analysis acknowledged was why it took six aircraft and their crews to demonstrate what the tactical commanders had identified before the operation began.

The eleven days of Linebacker II — with a pause on Christmas Day — produced approximately 729 B-52 sorties and a comparable number of supporting fighter and electronic warfare sorties. Fifteen B-52s were lost, with 12 other aircraft, and 93 airmen killed, captured, or missing. North Vietnam fired approximately 1,240 SA-2 missiles. The targeting concentrated on military infrastructure: rail yards, power plants, petroleum storage, air defense facilities, and the Paul Doumer Bridge over the Red River, which had been destroyed in Linebacker I and repaired. The civilian casualty figures for Linebacker II have been disputed since the operation ended. North Vietnamese government estimates cited in contemporary and subsequent sources were substantially higher than American estimates. The Bach Mai Hospital in Hanoi, struck on December 22, became an international focus of condemnation — the Air Force maintained the hospital was not deliberately targeted, and that the strikes occurred because Bach Mai was adjacent to a military airfield. International reaction to the bombing was strongly negative. Even British Prime Minister Edward Heath, a government aligned with the United States, described it as causing 'revulsion' in Britain.

Nixon described Linebacker II in his diary as forcing the North Vietnamese back to the table. The evidence for that interpretation is more ambiguous than the diary entry suggests. The Paris Peace Accords signed on January 27, 1973 were substantially similar in their terms to the October 1972 draft agreement that Kissinger had described as near-final — the agreement whose collapse produced Linebacker II. The historian Mark Clodfelter, in his 1989 study 'The Limits of Air Power,' argued that the bombing did not produce the settlement; rather, the settlement had been essentially agreed upon before the bombing began, and the bombing served different functions: reassuring Thieu that the United States remained committed, demonstrating to Nixon's domestic critics that he was pursuing peace from strength, and allowing both sides to claim they had not simply accepted the October terms unchanged. Clodfelter's interpretation has been contested by scholars who argue that the bombing genuinely altered Hanoi's negotiating calculus. The argument remains unresolved because Hanoi's internal deliberations in December 1972 have not been fully accessible to outside researchers.

The B-52s that bombed Hanoi in December 1972 were the same aircraft that had been striking targets in South Vietnam and along the Ho Chi Minh Trail since 1965. The difference in December 1972 was the target set — Hanoi and Haiphong, the political and economic centers of North Vietnam, within range of the most sophisticated air defense system in the world outside the Soviet Union and China. Strategic Air Command had built its entire institutional identity around the strategic bombing mission in Europe, and the B-52 was the centerpiece of that identity. Operating them in a conventional bombing role, in a high-threat environment, with mission profiles designed for a different theater, produced the loss rate of the first three nights. The adaptation that followed — varied routing, different altitudes, closer coordination between the B-52s and the F-105G Wild Weasel and EB-66 jamming aircraft — was a real-time revision of a doctrine that had not been designed for the Vietnam context. The revision worked. Fifteen B-52s in eleven days, against the losses SAC had modeled for a nuclear war with the Soviet Union, was within acceptable parameters. Whether the same parameters were appropriate for a conventional operation in a war that the United States was preparing to exit was a question the Air Force would argue about for years.

The Paris Peace Accords were signed on January 27, 1973, twenty-nine days after the last B-52 sortie of Linebacker II. Nixon declared that the accords achieved peace with honor. The South Vietnamese government of Nguyen Van Thieu accepted terms it had rejected in October with American pressure applied in the form of both private threats and private assurances of continued American support. Whether the agreement reflected Linebacker II's coercive effect on Hanoi, or Nixon's coercive effect on Thieu, or simply the exhaustion of both parties after eight years of fighting, the historians have not settled. What the record shows clearly is that the agreement signed in January 1973 left North Vietnamese forces inside South Vietnam, left the Thieu government in place but isolated, and set the conditions for the final offensive of April 1975. Linebacker II ended a phase of the war. It did not end the war.

shortForm.title: The SA-2 Over Hanoi: Why B-52s Were Vulnerable in December 1972
shortForm.excerpt: The SA-2 surface-to-air missile had been in North Vietnamese hands since 1965. B-52s carried jamming equipment specifically designed to defeat it. Five were still lost in the first three days of Linebacker II. The reason was not the missile. It was the tactics.
paragraphs: The SA-2 Guideline — NATO designation for the Soviet S-75 Dvina surface-to-air missile — had been deployed in North Vietnam since April 1965, when the first batteries became operational around Hanoi. American pilots had been dealing with the SA-2 for seven years by December 1972, and the electronic countermeasures suite carried by B-52s had been designed specifically to degrade the Fan Song radar that guided the missile. In principle, the technology was adequate. In practice, the loss rate in the first three days of Linebacker II demonstrated that the electronic countermeasures were being defeated — not by improvements in the SA-2 system itself, but by the predictability of the B-52 formations and the specific geometry of the post-target turns that SAC's mission planning had built into every sortie.

The SA-2's effective engagement envelope required the radar operator to track the target aircraft for a sustained period before launch. The B-52's jamming pods could break that track under most circumstances — but the pods were calibrated for aircraft flying in tight formation, and the jamming was most effective when all aircraft in the cell were at the same altitude and spacing. The post-target turn broke that geometry: the aircraft would separate slightly, reducing the jamming effectiveness at precisely the moment when radar operators, trained to anticipate the turn, were firing their missiles. North Vietnamese SA-2 operators had been trained by Soviet advisers and had been engaging American aircraft for years. They knew the standard B-52 tactics because those tactics had been used in earlier Arc Light strikes against targets in South Vietnam, where crews had practiced the same formations under much lower threat conditions. The tactics were predictable. The operators were good. The combination produced five B-52s lost in the first three days.

The adaptation after December 21 — varied routing, random altitude changes, modified post-target turn geometry — broke the predictability problem. Losses dropped from five in the first three days to two in the remaining eight days of the campaign. The lesson was straightforward: electronic countermeasures are a necessary but not sufficient condition for survival in a high-threat environment; they must be combined with tactical unpredictability to deny the threat system the sustained track it needs to engage effectively. The Air Force internalized that lesson and it shaped the development of both electronic warfare doctrine and stealth technology through the 1970s and 1980s. The B-2 Spirit, which flew its first combat missions over Kosovo in 1999, was designed in part around the insight that making an aircraft physically undetectable was more reliable than depending on jamming to break an adversary's radar track after the aircraft had already been acquired.

onThisDay.headline: Soviet Union Announces Shootdown of American U-2 Spy Plane
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1960, the Soviet Union publicly announced it had shot down an American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft over Soviet territory on May 1. Premier Khrushchev's announcement — delivered knowing the US would issue a false cover story — destroyed the Eisenhower administration's claim that the aircraft was a weather plane and collapsed the Paris Summit scheduled for May 16, 1960.
